competent

KOM-pih-tunt — think 'complete the tent': a competent camper can complete the tent setup without help. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Competent is having the skill and knowledge needed to do something successfully.

The new nurse proved competent, handling every patient calmly and correctly.

Example

On her first solo night shift, the technician notices the server crash immediately. Fully competent, she diagnoses the problem, restores the backups, and documents every step. No supervisor ever needs to be called.

Handling the crisis alone, without a single misstep, shows she has all the skill and knowledge the job requires. Unlike 'brilliant,' which implies extraordinary talent, competent means fully capable of doing the job well.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

capable: Capable means having the ability to do something — the raw potential is there. Competent goes further: a competent worker has the specific skill and knowledge the job requires and delivers reliably. A capable trainee might someday do the work; a competent electrician already does it well.

skilled: Skilled means having expertise from training or practice, and it often points at hands-on craft — a skilled welder, a skilled pianist. Competent is a judgment on the whole job: knowing enough and performing well enough to handle it successfully, even if no single skill dazzles.

qualified: Qualified means meeting the requirements for a task — the license, the degree, the certificate. Competent means actually having the skill and knowledge to do the job well. A person can be qualified on paper yet not competent in practice, or competent for years without the formal papers.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

incompetent: lacking the ability to do something properly

clumsy: awkward and lacking skill at a task

Where it sits · how expertly the job gets done

adequate → competent → masterful

adequate vs. competent: Adequate is weaker than competent — an adequate worker is barely good enough, while a competent one is solidly and reliably capable.

masterful vs. competent: Masterful is stronger than competent: a competent musician plays the piece correctly, but a masterful one commands it at an expert level.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — com-: together (Latin)

root — pet-: to seek, to strive (Latin)

suffix — -ent: in a state of (adjective-forming) (Latin)

Put it together: Latin competere meant 'to strive together, to be fitting.' Someone whose skills 'come together' to fit a task is suitable for it — competent.

Use the root in a new word: petition: Neighbors signed a petition seeking a new crosswalk near the school.

Word Building

Word Choice

Competent is solid praise meaning 'fully capable,' though in some contexts it can subtly imply 'capable but not exceptional.'
